paragraphs.source_en: After Clayton’s speech, the lecture hall erupted in a standing ovation like I had never experienced before. Literally, no one would sit down but just kept on clapping. In his own way, Clayton was challenging all of these Type A personalities who planned on building businesses and changing the world to think deeper than they had before about what truly defines success and to Begin With the End in Mind.

paragraphs.source_en: I hope you sense how strongly my father felt about the power of purpose and mission. As a young man, his grandfather, Stephen Mack Covey, tended sheep and was once trapped in a winter storm on the plains of Wyoming. It was 30 degrees below zero and, thinking he was going to die, he prayed, “God, if you will save me tonight, I promise to one day build a refuge on this very spot to protect other weary travelers.” Well, he made it through the night, and many years later built a hotel right there on the plains of Wyoming, which he called Covey’s Little America. Later, he successfully expanded to a second hotel in Salt Lake City. His son took over that business, and my dad was trained at a young age to be the next family hotel operator.

paragraphs.source_en: Even as a young man, Dad was always mission-driven. He had a short written mission statement, which he refined throughout his life. I don’t think he’d want me to share the exact wording, but basically, it was the idea of unlocking human potential and flooding the world with principle-centered leadership. He saw himself as a pathfinder, a trailblazer, a paradigm breaker. That was the role he envisioned: bringing principle-centered leadership to the world and unleashing human potential.
